Rectifier cables

1. Cable management to the electrode bars.

2. Make up all connections with the proper hardware.
2.1 Most electrode bars take a 10mm 1.5 bolt.
2.2 Exceptions:
    a. The center bars in tanks 311, 223, 211, 129 and 117.
    b. The electro clean tanks have 6 bars that have 3/8-16 threaded holes.
2.3 To tell whether a hole is 3/8 or 10mm, try to insert a 10mm bolt. Does it fit and can it be turned in by hand?
    Yes: the hole is 10mm.
    No: the hole is 3/8.
2.4 NOTE: A 3/8 bolt will fit into a 10mm hole but should not be installed that way. That is why the test is done with the 10mm bolt.

3. Route the cables from the bars over the backs of the tanks. Insert spacers that will not melt (cardboard or wood) between the steam lines and the cables. The last photo is an example of the expected final cable routing.

4. Zip tie the cables together in bundles as you move from the electrode bars down into the aluminum cable tray in the basement.

1. Build unistrut mounts
1.1 Unistrut is intended to be cut to 32 inches long. There is enough to do all tanks.
1.2 Install the 90 degree brackets provided just as done on the first example tank, tank 211.
1.3 The brackets ordered have 1/2 inch holes, so use the provided 3/8" stainless flat washers, as done on tank 211.

2. Mount coils to the new mounts and install in tanks
2.1 Pull the coil from the tank and remove the original hanger.
2.2 Note which direction the coil goes in the tank so the brackets are not installed in the wrong direction.
2.3 Install the unistrut brackets on the coil. The brackets can be mounted to the coil spaced 12 inches apart and centered on the center position of the center electrode bar, just as done on example tank 211.
2.4 Height must put the threaded connections above the rim of the tank, but not higher than practically necessary for routing the piping under or through the fume hoods.
2.5 Do not penetrate the duct section (fume carrying cavity) of the fume hoods. The wings on either side can be cut to fit piping through.
2.6 If you must cut through the wings of the fume hood, drill two 2-inch holes with a hole saw, centered with the stainless pipe nipples, then make a cut between the tops and bottoms of those holes to create a clean horizontal oval shape.

3. Install stainless nipples and fittings
3.1 Install the stainless fittings as done on the example tank.
3.2 90 degree elbows face away from the tank, to the side.
3.3 Install 3 in and 6 in nipples in each 90 degree elbow.
3.4 90 degree elbow to both nipples facing toward the back of the tank.
3.5 12 inch nipples go horizontal toward the rear of the tank.
3.6 Install 90 degree elbows onto the 12 inch nipples, pointing down. Plastic starts at this point. Stainless-to-plastic connection points are always female stainless and male plastic.

4. Connect to plastic

Steam system leak test.

Read [Steam Line System Safety](/steam-safety.html) before starting.

1. The process

1.1 Testing steam supply for an individual plating line
    a. Open the main steam supply valve in the boiler room. (This valve should be closed any time you leave the building.)
    b. Walk the line you will be testing and verify all steam valves are closed.
    c. Open the valve that supplies steam to the line you are testing. Always open all steam valves slowly.
    d. Walk the steam line looking for any smoke or steam leaks. If issues are found, turn the steam supply valve off and solve the issues. This tests the steam supply line for one of the plating lines only.
    e. Once you can leave the steam supply open with no smoke or steam leaks, you are ready to continue. If you still have issues, continue making repairs until they are all fixed.
    f. Open the end of supply line steam trap. This allows condensate to flow.
    g. Make sure the condensate return pump can take away condensate.
    h. At this point the steam supply line has been tested. Now test all the piping connections on each individual tank.

1.2 Testing steam lines for individual tanks
    a. Only the manual valves will be tested first.
    b. Open the solenoid valve's bypass valve. This applies steam to the tank's heating coil. Check for leaks.
    c. Open the valve on the outlet of the steam trap first, then open the valve on the inlet side of the steam trap. Steam should reach the trap, and as condensate forms it should start to flow through the trap.
    d. Once you have heard the steam trap cycle and there are no leaks, test the piping to the automatic valve.
    e. Open each of the manual isolation valves on each side of the automatic brass valve.
    f. You are now testing the full steam system of this tank except the operation of the automatic valve. The automatic valve will be tested later.
    g. Close the automatic valve's bypass valve, then close each of the other valves in the system, all the way down to the valve on the outlet side of the steam trap.
    h. This tank's steam system has now been tested. Proceed to the next tank.

2. Document all issues found. Fix any steam leaks found.

3. Monitor the condensate return tank. Make sure it is powered on and pumping condensate back to the boiler. It has a sight glass so you can monitor the level. Verify all valves are open and you can feel a temperature change to confirm condensate is moving through the pipe.
